questions.stem: In the food web shown, which organism occupies more than one trophic level?
choices: The deer
The grasshopper
The hawk
The rabbit
questions.explanation: The hawk eats mice and rabbits (making it a secondary consumer) and snakes, which eat mice (making it a tertiary consumer). The deer, grasshopper, and rabbit eat only producers.

questions.stem: Wolves are removed from the ecosystem shown. Which change is most likely in the following years?
choices: The deer population increases, and the shrub population decreases.
The deer population decreases, and the shrub population increases.
The grass population increases because there are fewer rabbits.
The snake population decreases because there are fewer wolves.
questions.explanation: Without wolves, predation on deer and rabbits falls, so those herbivores increase and consume more shrubs. A predator's removal can cascade down through several trophic levels.

questions.stem: Approximately what percentage of the energy at each trophic level is transferred to the next level in the pyramid shown?
questions.explanation: Each level holds one tenth of the energy of the level below, for example \(\tfrac{2{,}000}{20{,}000}\). The rest is used for cellular respiration and lost as heat, or never eaten or digested.

questions.stem: A person eats \(1\) kg of beef or \(1\) kg of grain. Based on the pyramid shown, which statement best explains why a diet based on grain can feed more people from the same farmland?
choices: Grain contains more energy per kilogram than beef.
Eating producers directly avoids the roughly \(90\%\) energy loss that occurs when crops are fed to livestock.
Cattle store all of the energy they eat in their muscles.
Producers use less sunlight than consumers.
questions.explanation: Energy available to humans who eat grain-fed animals has passed through one more trophic level. Each transfer loses about 90 percent of the energy, mostly as heat from respiration.

questions.stem: In a forest, gross primary productivity is \(3{,}200\text{ g/m}^2\text{/yr}\), and the producers use \(1{,}100\text{ g/m}^2\text{/yr}\) for cellular respiration. What is the net primary productivity?
questions.explanation: \(\text{NPP}=\text{GPP}-R_A=3{,}200-1{,}100=2{,}100\). NPP is the energy available to consumers as biomass.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the open ocean has such low net primary productivity per square meter, even though it receives abundant sunlight?
choices: Phytoplankton cannot photosynthesize in salt water.
Light cannot penetrate the ocean surface.
Ocean water is too warm for photosynthesis.
Surface waters of the open ocean are poor in nutrients, especially nitrogen and phosphorus, which limits phytoplankton growth.
questions.explanation: Without upwelling or runoff, nutrients sink below the sunlit zone. Estuaries, by contrast, receive nutrients from rivers, which is why their productivity rivals that of rainforests.

questions.stem: Although the open ocean has a very low productivity per square meter, it accounts for a large share of Earth's total net primary productivity. Which statement explains this?
choices: The open ocean covers a much larger area than any land biome.
The open ocean has the highest productivity per square meter.
Ocean producers are larger than land plants.
The graph shows total productivity, not productivity per area.
questions.explanation: Total productivity is productivity per area multiplied by area. The open ocean covers more than half of Earth's surface.

questions.stem: Which location in the table is most likely a tropical rainforest?
choices: X
Y
W
Z
questions.explanation: Tropical rainforests are warm year-round with very heavy rainfall. Rapid decomposition and uptake leave the soils nutrient-poor, while the vegetation forms many layers.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches locations in the table with biomes?
choices: X is boreal forest, and Z is tundra.
Y is temperate grassland, and Z is temperate deciduous forest.
W is a savanna, and Y is a chaparral.
X is tundra, and Z is boreal forest (taiga).
questions.explanation: Permafrost and low-growing plants indicate tundra. Long cold winters with dense coniferous trees and acidic soils indicate taiga. Location Y, with very little rain and drought-adapted plants, is a desert.

questions.stem: Which process converts atmospheric \(\mathrm{N_{2}}\) into a form that plants can use?
choices: Denitrification, carried out by bacteria in wet soils
Ammonification, carried out by decomposers
Nitrogen fixation, carried out by bacteria such as those in the root nodules of legumes
Assimilation by plant leaves
questions.explanation: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert \(\mathrm{N_{2}}\) into ammonia or ammonium. Lightning and the industrial production of fertilizer also fix nitrogen.

questions.stem: Which process returns nitrogen from the soil to the atmosphere?
choices: Nitrification, in which bacteria convert ammonium to nitrate
Denitrification, in which bacteria convert nitrate to \(\mathrm{N_{2}}\) gas
Nitrogen fixation, in which bacteria convert \(\mathrm{N_{2}}\) to ammonia
Assimilation, in which plants take up nitrate
questions.explanation: Denitrifying bacteria thrive in waterlogged, low-oxygen soils, where they use nitrate in place of oxygen and release nitrogen gas.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why phosphorus is often the limiting nutrient in freshwater ecosystems?
choices: The phosphorus cycle has no significant atmospheric component, and phosphorus is released slowly by the weathering of rock.
Phosphorus is rapidly lost to the atmosphere.
Bacteria convert phosphorus into a gas.
Organisms need more phosphorus than any other element.
questions.explanation: Because phosphorus is not stored in the air, it enters ecosystems mainly through weathering, which is slow. Adding phosphate from fertilizers or detergents can therefore cause algal blooms.

questions.stem: Which reservoir stores the most carbon for the longest time?
choices: The atmosphere
Living plants
Sedimentary rock, such as limestone
Surface ocean water
questions.explanation: Carbon in sedimentary rock and fossil fuels can remain for millions of years. Burning fossil fuels moves this long-stored carbon quickly into the atmosphere.

questions.stem: Which pair of processes moves carbon in opposite directions between the atmosphere and living organisms?
choices: Photosynthesis removes \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) from the air, and cellular respiration returns it.
Combustion and respiration both remove \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) from the air.
Photosynthesis and decomposition both remove \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) from the air.
Respiration and sedimentation both add \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) to the air.
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis fixes carbon into sugars, and organisms release it by breaking those sugars down. Decomposition and combustion also release carbon.

questions.stem: Which process transfers water from the leaves of plants to the atmosphere?
choices: Infiltration
Condensation
Runoff
Transpiration
questions.explanation: Plants release water vapor through their stomata. Together with evaporation, it is called evapotranspiration, which is a major source of moisture in rainforests.

questions.stem: Remora fish attach to sharks and eat scraps of the sharks' meals, apparently without affecting the sharks. Which type of relationship is this?
choices: Mutualism
Commensalism
Parasitism
Competition
questions.explanation: In commensalism, one species benefits while the other is unaffected. In mutualism, both benefit; in parasitism, one is harmed.

questions.stem: Two warbler species feed on insects in the same spruce trees, but one feeds near the tops of the trees and the other near the trunk. Which concept does this illustrate?
choices: Mutualism, which benefits both species
Resource partitioning, which reduces competition
Predation, which limits both populations
Competitive exclusion, in which one species is eliminated
questions.explanation: Dividing a resource by location or timing allows similar species to coexist. Without partitioning, one species might outcompete the other.

questions.stem: In a pond ecosystem, which organism is a primary consumer?
choices: Algae that photosynthesize
Bass that eat small fish
Bacteria that decompose dead matter
Zooplankton that eat algae
questions.explanation: Primary consumers eat producers. Algae are producers, bass are higher-level consumers, and bacteria are decomposers.

questions.stem: Which change would most likely increase the gross primary productivity of a lake?
choices: Increased sunlight reaching the water because sediment has settled out
Increased cloudiness
A decrease in nitrogen and phosphorus inputs
Colder water temperatures
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis is limited by light and nutrients. Clearer water allows more light to reach phytoplankton and submerged plants.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels?
choices: Top predators are always too large to be eaten.
Matter cannot be recycled through more levels.
So little energy remains at the top levels that it cannot support another population.
Producers cannot support more than four consumers.
questions.explanation: With about 10 percent passing to each level, a fifth level receives roughly \(0.01\%\) of the energy fixed by producers.

questions.stem: A farmer applies nitrogen fertilizer before a heavy rainstorm. Where is much of the nitrate most likely to end up?
choices: In the atmosphere as \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\)
In the bedrock as minerals
In the crops, because nitrate is not water soluble
In nearby streams and groundwater, because nitrate is soluble and leaches easily
questions.explanation: Nitrate ions dissolve in water and are not held well by soil particles. Runoff and leaching carry them into waterways, where they can cause eutrophication.

questions.stem: Which factor most directly determines the distribution of terrestrial biomes around the world?
choices: The number of species present
The type of animals present
Temperature and precipitation
The depth of the soil
questions.explanation: Climate determines which plants can grow, and the plants define the biome. Latitude, elevation, and ocean currents affect climate.

questions.stem: Which aquatic ecosystem is characterized by a mix of fresh and salt water, high productivity, and its role as a nursery for many fish?
choices: Open ocean
Estuary
Coral reef
Freshwater lake
questions.explanation: Where rivers meet the sea, estuaries receive nutrients from land and support salt marshes and mangroves. Many commercially important fish spend their early lives there.

figure.alt: Table of the number of individuals of four species, A through D, in two communities. Community 1 has 25 of each species. Community 2 has 85 of species A and 5 each of species B, C, and D

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares the two communities in the table?
choices: They have the same species richness, but community 1 has greater species evenness and therefore greater diversity.
Community 2 has greater species richness.
They have the same diversity, because they contain the same species.
Community 2 has greater diversity because it has more individuals of species A.
questions.explanation: Richness is the number of species, four in each. Evenness describes how equally individuals are distributed among species. Community 2 is dominated by species A.

figure.alt: Table of the number of individuals of four species, A through D, in two communities. Community 1 has 25 of each species. Community 2 has 85 of species A and 5 each of species B, C, and D

questions.stem: A disease that kills most individuals of species A spreads into both communities in the table. Which community is more likely to maintain its overall function?
choices: Community 2, because it has more individuals of species A
Both are equally affected, because both contain species A
Community 1, because no single species dominates it
Neither, because all four species would die
questions.explanation: In community 1, losing species A removes only a quarter of the individuals. In community 2, it removes 85 percent, so the community is much less resilient.

figure.alt: Graph of number of species against island area for islands near the mainland and far from it. Both curves rise steeply for small islands and then more slowly. At every island size, islands near the mainland have more species: at 100 km², about 42 species near versus about 25 far away

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the graph?
choices: Larger islands and islands closer to the mainland support more species.
Island size has no effect on the number of species.
Islands far from the mainland have more species because there is less competition.
The number of species increases at the same rate for all island sizes.
questions.explanation: Larger islands offer more habitats and support larger populations, which lowers extinction rates. Closer islands receive more immigrants. Habitat fragments act like islands in the same way.

questions.stem: A forest is cut into small, isolated patches by roads and farmland. Based on the graph, what is the most likely effect on the forest's species?
choices: Each patch will gain species because of increased edge habitat.
The number of species will remain the same, because the forest still exists.
Only the number of producers will change.
Each patch will lose species over time, because small, isolated areas have higher extinction rates and fewer immigrants.
questions.explanation: Habitat fragmentation turns continuous habitat into "islands." Wildlife corridors connecting patches can reduce this loss by allowing movement between them.

questions.stem: The fish population shown is exposed to water at \(32^\circ\text{C}\). Which response is expected?
choices: The population grows at its maximum rate.
Individuals experience physiological stress, so growth and reproduction decline.
All of the fish die immediately.
The fish are unaffected because they are within their range of tolerance.
questions.explanation: \(32^\circ\text{C}\) lies in zone Q, a zone of physiological stress. Individuals can survive there but with reduced growth, reproduction, and resistance to disease.

questions.stem: Climate change raises the average water temperature in the fish's habitat from \(20^\circ\text{C}\) to \(30^\circ\text{C}\). Which response by the species is most likely?
choices: Its population increases, because its optimal range is extended.
Its population declines, or it shifts its range toward cooler water if it can.
It adapts immediately, because individuals change their tolerance.
It is unaffected, because \(30^\circ\text{C}\) is below its upper limit.
questions.explanation: The species' optimal range ends near \(29^\circ\text{C}\). Populations can move to new areas, but species with limited dispersal or long generations may not adapt fast enough.

questions.stem: Sea otters eat sea urchins, which eat kelp. When otters were hunted nearly to extinction, kelp forests disappeared from many coastlines. Which term best describes the otter?
choices: An indicator species
A pioneer species
An invasive species
A keystone species
questions.explanation: A keystone species has an effect on its ecosystem much larger than its abundance would suggest. Without otters, urchin populations exploded and overgrazed the kelp.

questions.stem: Which describes primary succession?
choices: Lichens and mosses colonize bare rock left after a glacier retreats, slowly building soil.
Grasses regrow in a field after a farm is abandoned.
A forest regrows after a wildfire burns the trees but leaves the soil.
Shrubs replace grasses in a field after logging.
questions.explanation: Primary succession begins where there is no soil. Secondary succession occurs where soil remains after a disturbance, so it proceeds much faster.

questions.stem: How does species diversity usually change during succession in a temperate forest?
choices: It decreases steadily from the pioneer stage.
It remains constant throughout succession.
It generally increases over time, often peaking in intermediate stages.
It is highest immediately after a disturbance.
questions.explanation: Over time, soil depth and habitat complexity increase, supporting more species. Some studies find diversity peaks before the late-stage community, when a few dominant species take over.

questions.stem: Mayfly and stonefly larvae are found in a stream, while they are absent from a nearby stream. What is the most likely conclusion?
choices: The stream without the larvae has higher water quality.
Both streams have the same water quality.
The larvae increase water pollution.
The stream with the larvae has higher water quality, including high dissolved oxygen.
questions.explanation: These insects are indicator species that are sensitive to pollution and low oxygen. Their presence suggests good water quality.

questions.stem: A wetland filters pollutants from water, reduces flooding by absorbing water, and provides habitat for fish. What are these benefits called?
choices: Ecological footprints
Limiting factors
Ecosystem services
Biotic potential
questions.explanation: Ecosystem services are benefits that people receive from natural systems. Destroying wetlands removes these services, which can be expensive to replace with technology.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a regulating ecosystem service?
choices: Timber harvested for lumber
Forests absorbing \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) and moderating climate
Fish caught for food
Recreational hiking
questions.explanation: Regulating services include climate regulation, pollination, and flood control. Timber and fish are provisioning services, and hiking is a cultural service.

questions.stem: A population of cheetahs has very low genetic diversity after a population bottleneck. What is the greatest risk?
choices: The population may be unable to adapt to new diseases or environmental changes.
The population will immediately become extinct.
The population will grow too quickly.
The population will have greater fitness.
questions.explanation: Genetic diversity provides variation for natural selection to act on. Low diversity also increases inbreeding, which can lead to harmful traits.

questions.stem: Over many generations, the frequency of pesticide resistance increases in an insect population after repeated pesticide use. What explains this?
choices: Individual insects developed resistance during their lifetimes.
The pesticide caused mutations for resistance.
Natural selection: resistant individuals survived and reproduced, passing on resistance.
The pesticide became less toxic over time.
questions.explanation: Resistance existed in a few individuals before spraying. The pesticide removed susceptible insects, so resistant ones made up more of each generation.

questions.stem: Which statement about natural disruptions to ecosystems is correct?
choices: They can be periodic, episodic, or random, and some species depend on them, such as plants whose seeds open after fire.
They always lead to permanent ecosystem collapse.
They occur only because of human activity.
They never change the species present.
questions.explanation: Fires, floods, and storms reset succession and create new habitats. Fire suppression can lead to the buildup of fuel and more intense fires.

questions.stem: Which ecosystem is likely to be most resilient to a disturbance?
choices: One dominated by a single species
One with low genetic diversity
One with few trophic levels
One with high species diversity and many species filling similar roles
questions.explanation: When several species perform similar functions, the loss of one can be offset by others. Monocultures, such as single-crop fields, are especially vulnerable.

questions.stem: Which practice most directly preserves genetic diversity within a crop species?
choices: Planting a single high-yield variety in every field
Seed banks that store many varieties of the crop
Using more chemical fertilizer
Increasing irrigation
questions.explanation: Storing many varieties preserves traits, such as resistance to drought or disease, that may become important. Monocultures of one variety reduce genetic diversity.

questions.stem: Which statement about the current rate of extinction is supported by scientific evidence?
choices: It is lower than the background rate.
It is much higher than the natural background rate, mainly because of human activities such as habitat loss.
It is caused mainly by asteroid impacts.
Extinctions no longer occur.
questions.explanation: Scientists estimate current extinction rates are tens to hundreds of times the background rate, leading many to describe a sixth mass extinction.

questions.stem: A non-native plant spreads rapidly in a new region because none of its natural herbivores live there. Which concept best explains its success?
choices: Mutualism with native herbivores
Primary succession
A low biotic potential
Release from the predators and herbivores that limited it in its native range
questions.explanation: Invasive species often succeed because the natural enemies that controlled them are absent. Without those limits, they outcompete native species.

questions.stem: Which species is most likely to survive a major environmental change?
choices: A generalist with a broad niche, such as a raccoon
A specialist that eats only one kind of plant
A species that lives in a single isolated habitat
A species with a long generation time and few offspring
questions.explanation: Generalists can use a variety of food and habitats, so they cope better when conditions change. Specialists are vulnerable if their resource or habitat disappears.

questions.stem: Corals turn white and may die when ocean temperatures stay \(1\)–\(2^\circ\text{C}\) above their normal summer maximum for several weeks. Which best explains this?
choices: Warm water dissolves the coral skeleton instantly.
Algae grow so quickly that they smother the coral.
Heat stress causes corals to expel the symbiotic algae that supply most of their food through photosynthesis.
Corals stop feeding because fish leave the reef.
questions.explanation: Corals and their zooxanthellae are mutualists. Outside the coral's range of tolerance the relationship breaks down, causing bleaching; prolonged bleaching leads to starvation.

questions.stem: A population of squirrels is split by the formation of a canyon. Over many generations, the two groups can no longer interbreed. Which process occurred?
choices: Sympatric speciation, without geographic isolation
Artificial selection by humans
Convergent evolution of unrelated species
Allopatric speciation, caused by geographic isolation
questions.explanation: Separated populations experience different mutations, selection pressures, and genetic drift. Over time they become reproductively isolated, forming separate species.

questions.stem: Which characteristics define a biodiversity hotspot?
choices: Very few species but large populations of each
Only protected national parks
A large number of endemic species and a high degree of habitat loss
Areas with the highest human population density
questions.explanation: Hotspots, such as Madagascar, contain many species found nowhere else and have lost much of their original habitat. Protecting them conserves a large share of global biodiversity in a small area.

questions.stem: Which type of organism is most likely to have survivorship curve III?
choices: Humans in developed countries
Oysters, which release millions of eggs with no parental care
Elephants, which raise few offspring with extensive care
Songbirds, which have a constant chance of dying at any age
questions.explanation: Curve III shows very high mortality early in life. Producing huge numbers of offspring without parental care is characteristic of r-selected species.

Curve II declines in a straight line on the log scale. Curve III drops steeply at the start of life and then levels off with few survivors

questions.stem: Curve I in the graph is most typical of which kind of species?
choices: K-selected species, which have few offspring and provide extensive parental care
r-selected species, which have many offspring
Species with a constant risk of death throughout life
Species with no parental care
questions.explanation: Curve I shows high survival until old age. Investment in a small number of offspring makes each one likely to survive to adulthood.

questions.stem: At which point in the graph is the population growing fastest, and why?

C, because the population is largest
B, because the population is large but resources are not yet limiting
Growth is the same at all points.
questions.explanation: In logistic growth, the growth rate is greatest at half the carrying capacity. Early on there are few individuals to reproduce; near K, limited resources slow growth.

questions.stem: What causes the population's growth rate to approach zero near point C?
choices: Density-dependent factors, such as competition for food and space, increase as the population nears carrying capacity.
Density-independent factors, such as a sudden freeze.
The population runs out of individuals capable of reproducing.
Birth rates increase.
questions.explanation: As the population approaches K, resource scarcity and other density-dependent factors lower birth rates and raise death rates until they are about equal.

questions.stem: A deer population overshoots its carrying capacity after predators are removed. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: The population stays above the carrying capacity indefinitely.
The carrying capacity increases to match the population.
The population becomes extinct immediately.
The population declines sharply as the deer overgraze vegetation, possibly lowering the carrying capacity.
questions.explanation: Overshoot damages the resources the population depends on. A die-off typically follows, and the degraded habitat may support fewer deer than before.

questions.stem: Which set of traits describes an r-selected species?
choices: Few large offspring, late maturity, and long life span
Many small offspring, early maturity, short life span, and little parental care
Populations that stay near carrying capacity
Slow reproduction and extensive parental care
questions.explanation: r-selected species reproduce quickly and are often good colonizers and invasive species. K-selected species, such as elephants, invest heavily in few offspring.

questions.stem: What is the growth rate of the population in stage 3 of the figure, expressed as a percentage?
questions.explanation: \(25-10=15\) per 1,000 people per year, which is \(\tfrac{15}{1000}=1.5\%\). Using the rates directly as percentages gives the incorrect \(15\%\).

questions.stem: A country's population grows at \(2\%\) per year. Using the rule of 70, about how long will it take for the population to double?
choices: \(140\) years
\(70\) years
\(20\) years
\(35\) years
questions.explanation: Doubling time \(\approx\dfrac{70}{\text{percent growth rate}}=\dfrac{70}{2}=35\) years. The rule applies to exponential growth at a constant rate.

questions.stem: A city of \(500{,}000\) people has \(12{,}000\) births, \(4{,}000\) deaths, \(3{,}000\) immigrants, and \(1{,}000\) emigrants in a year. What is its percentage growth rate?
Which factor is most strongly associated with a decline in a country's total fertility rate?
choices: A lower average age of marriage
Greater access to education and employment for women
Higher infant mortality
Greater reliance on children for farm labor
questions.explanation: Educated women tend to marry later, have more economic options, and have greater access to family planning. Higher infant mortality tends to raise fertility.

questions.stem: Why is replacement-level fertility about \(2.1\) rather than exactly \(2.0\) children per woman in developed countries?
choices: Some children die before reaching reproductive age, and slightly more boys than girls are born.
Each person must be replaced by more than one child.
Immigration requires extra births.
Women have, on average, two children.
questions.explanation: Two children replace the parents, and the extra 0.1 accounts for early deaths and the sex ratio. Where child mortality is higher, the replacement level is higher.

questions.stem: A country reaches replacement-level fertility, yet its population continues to grow for decades. Which best explains this?
choices: The death rate is increasing.
Immigration has stopped.
A large share of the population is still young and entering its childbearing years.
The total fertility rate is below 1.
questions.explanation: Population momentum occurs because many people are born before fertility falls. They still have children, even at replacement level, until the age structure evens out.

questions.stem: Which factor limiting a population is density-dependent?
choices: A disease that spreads more easily when individuals live close together
A hurricane that destroys habitat
A severe drought
A volcanic eruption
questions.explanation: The effect of a density-dependent factor increases as the population becomes more crowded. Natural disasters affect populations regardless of their density.

questions.stem: Populations of snowshoe hares and lynx rise and fall in repeating cycles, with lynx peaks following hare peaks. Which best explains the timing?
choices: Hares eat lynx.
Both populations respond only to weather.
Lynx populations cause hare populations to increase.
Lynx populations increase after hares become abundant, and then decline after hares become scarce.
questions.explanation: Predator populations lag behind prey populations because they depend on the prey for food. Hare populations are also affected by their own food supply.

questions.stem: Which statement about the history of human population growth is correct?
choices: Growth has been constant throughout history.
Growth was slow for most of history and then became nearly exponential after the Industrial Revolution.
The population declined during the Industrial Revolution.
The population has already reached a stable carrying capacity.
questions.explanation: Improvements in agriculture, sanitation, and medicine sharply lowered death rates, especially since about 1800. Growth rates have declined since the 1960s, though the population is still increasing.

questions.stem: A population of \(1{,}000\) grows at \(7\%\) per year. Using the rule of 70, about how large will it be after \(30\) years?
questions.explanation: The doubling time is \(\tfrac{70}{7}=10\) years, so 30 years is three doublings: \(1{,}000\times 2^3=8{,}000\). Linear growth would give only \(3{,}100\).

questions.stem: How have humans increased Earth's carrying capacity for humans?
choices: By reducing their consumption of resources
By lowering birth rates to zero
By relying only on renewable resources
Through technologies such as fertilizers, irrigation, and modern medicine
questions.explanation: The Green Revolution and medical advances increased food supplies and survival. Many scientists argue that this increase depends on unsustainable use of resources such as fossil fuels and groundwater.

questions.stem: Which organism best fits a Type II survivorship curve, with a roughly constant chance of dying at every age?
choices: Many songbirds
Humans in a wealthy country
Sea turtles
Dandelions
questions.explanation: Type II species face a similar risk of death throughout life, often from predation. Humans in wealthy countries follow Type I, and sea turtles and dandelions follow Type III.

Layer 4, the thermosphere

questions.stem: In which layer shown does almost all weather occur?
choices: Layer 2, the stratosphere
Layer 3, the mesosphere
Layer 1, the troposphere
Layer 4, the thermosphere
questions.explanation: The troposphere is heated from below by Earth's surface, so warm air rises and cools, causing convection, clouds, and precipitation. It contains about 75 percent of the atmosphere's mass.

questions.stem: Which horizon shown is most important for growing crops and is most vulnerable to erosion?
choices: B
A
C
R
questions.explanation: The A horizon, or topsoil, contains humus mixed with minerals and most of the soil's organisms and nutrients. Its loss by erosion reduces fertility.

figure.alt: Table of soil texture for three samples. Sample 1: 85 percent sand, 10 percent silt, 5 percent clay. Sample 2: 40 percent sand, 40 percent silt, 20 percent clay. Sample 3: 10 percent sand, 30 percent silt, 60 percent clay

questions.stem: Which soil sample in the table has the highest water-holding capacity and the lowest permeability?
choices: Sample 3
Sample 1
Sample 2
All three are equal.
questions.explanation: Clay particles are tiny and pack closely, leaving small pores that hold water tightly and drain slowly. Sandy sample 1 drains fastest and holds the least water.

figure.alt: Table of soil texture for three samples. Sample 1: 85 percent sand, 10 percent silt, 5 percent clay. Sample 2: 40 percent sand, 40 percent silt, 20 percent clay. Sample 3: 10 percent sand, 30 percent silt, 60 percent clay

questions.stem: Which sample in the table is closest to a loam, which is often considered ideal for agriculture?
choices: Sample 1
Sample 3
Sample 2
None of them
questions.explanation: Loam combines sand, silt, and clay so that it drains well while holding enough water and nutrients. Sample 2 is the most balanced mixture.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the climates on sides A and B of the mountain?
choices: Side A is wet, because rising air cools and drops its moisture, and side B is dry, because the descending air warms.
Side A is dry and side B is wet.
Both sides receive equal rainfall.
Side B is wetter because it is farther from the ocean.
questions.explanation: Moist air rising on the windward side cools and condenses, producing rain. Air descending on the leeward side warms and holds its remaining moisture, creating a rain shadow desert.

questions.stem: Along which type of plate boundary do the deepest ocean trenches and many explosive volcanoes form?
choices: Divergent boundaries
Transform boundaries
The middle of plates
Convergent boundaries where an oceanic plate is subducted
questions.explanation: At subduction zones, the denser oceanic plate sinks into the mantle, forming trenches. Melting above the descending plate feeds volcanoes, as along the Pacific Ring of Fire.

questions.stem: The San Andreas Fault, where two plates slide past each other, is an example of which kind of boundary, and what hazard is most associated with it?
choices: A divergent boundary, associated with volcanoes
A transform boundary, associated with earthquakes
A convergent boundary, associated with mountain building
A transform boundary, associated with tsunamis from subduction
questions.explanation: At transform boundaries, plates move horizontally past each other, building stress that is released suddenly as earthquakes.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the equator receives more solar energy per square meter than the poles?
choices: The equator is closer to the sun.
Sunlight strikes the equator nearly directly, while it strikes the poles at a low angle and is spread over a larger area.
The poles have more clouds.
The equator has a thinner atmosphere.
questions.explanation: At low angles, the same beam of sunlight covers more surface and passes through more atmosphere. Differences in distance from the sun are negligible.

questions.stem: What causes Earth's seasons?
choices: Changes in Earth's distance from the sun
Changes in the sun's energy output
Ocean currents
The tilt of Earth's axis, which changes the angle and duration of sunlight through the year
questions.explanation: Because Earth's axis is tilted about \(23.5^\circ\), each hemisphere receives more direct sunlight and longer days when tilted toward the sun.

questions.stem: Which statement explains why many of the world's large deserts lie near \(30^\circ\) north and south latitude?
choices: Air that rose at the equator descends near \(30^\circ\), warming and drying as it sinks.
These latitudes receive the least sunlight.
Ocean currents carry dry air to these latitudes.
These latitudes have the highest mountains.
questions.explanation: In Hadley cells, warm, moist air rises at the equator and drops its rain. The dry air then sinks near \(30^\circ\), producing high pressure and little precipitation.

questions.stem: Which describes typical conditions during an El Niño event?
choices: Trade winds strengthen, and upwelling off South America increases.
The western Pacific becomes warmer and wetter than usual.
Trade winds weaken, warm water spreads to the eastern Pacific, and upwelling off South America decreases.
Ocean temperatures stay the same, but rainfall increases everywhere.
questions.explanation: With weaker upwelling, fewer nutrients reach the surface off Peru, reducing fish populations. Rainfall patterns shift, bringing floods to some regions and droughts to others.

questions.stem: A city draws its drinking water from a river. Which action would best protect the water's quality?
choices: Building more roads near the river
Clearing vegetation along the riverbanks
Increasing the use of fertilizer upstream
Protecting forests and wetlands throughout the river's watershed
questions.explanation: A watershed is all the land that drains into a body of water. Vegetation filters pollutants and reduces erosion, so protecting the watershed protects the water supply.

questions.stem: Which factor most directly speeds the formation of soil from parent material?
choices: Erosion by wind
Compaction by heavy machinery
Weathering by water, temperature changes, and living organisms
Removal of vegetation
questions.explanation: Physical, chemical, and biological weathering break rock into smaller particles, and organisms add organic matter. Soil forms very slowly, often centuries per centimeter.

questions.stem: Which soil property most directly affects the soil's ability to hold nutrients such as potassium and calcium ions?
choices: The amount of sand
Clay and humus content, because their particles carry negative charges that attract positive ions
The color of the soil
The depth of the C horizon
questions.explanation: Clay and humus have large surface areas with negative charges that hold cations and keep them from leaching. Sandy soils lose nutrients quickly.

questions.stem: Which statement about the rock cycle is correct?
choices: Igneous rock forms from cooled magma, and any type of rock can become sedimentary, metamorphic, or igneous over time.
Sedimentary rock forms only from magma.
Metamorphic rock forms when rock melts completely.
Rocks cannot change from one type to another.
questions.explanation: Weathering, heat, pressure, and melting continuously transform rocks. Metamorphic rock forms from heat and pressure without melting.

questions.stem: Which statement about the global ocean conveyor belt (thermohaline circulation) is correct?
choices: It is driven only by wind.
It moves only surface water.
It is driven by differences in water density caused by temperature and salinity, and it moves heat around the planet.
Fresh meltwater would strengthen it.
questions.explanation: Cold, salty water sinks in the North Atlantic and flows along the ocean floor. Large inputs of fresh water could reduce sinking and weaken the circulation.

questions.stem: Which gas makes up the largest percentage of Earth's atmosphere?
choices: Nitrogen, about \(78\%\)
Oxygen, about \(78\%\)
Carbon dioxide, about \(21\%\)
Argon, about \(21\%\)
questions.explanation: Dry air is about 78 percent nitrogen, 21 percent oxygen, and 0.9 percent argon. Carbon dioxide is about 0.04 percent, yet it has a large effect on climate.

questions.stem: Which statement explains why Iceland has many volcanoes?
choices: It sits on a transform boundary.
It is located on a subduction zone.
It is in the middle of a stable plate.
It sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, a divergent boundary, above a hot spot.
questions.explanation: At divergent boundaries, plates pull apart and magma rises to fill the gap. A hot spot beneath Iceland adds even more volcanic activity.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the Coriolis effect?
choices: Earth's tilt causes winds to blow toward the poles.
Earth's rotation deflects moving air and water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
Warm air rises at the poles.
The moon's gravity creates prevailing winds.
questions.explanation: The Coriolis effect turns winds from the Hadley cells into the trade winds and westerlies, and it shapes the rotation of ocean gyres.

questions.stem: Which statement about an unconfined aquifer is correct?
choices: It lies between two layers of impermeable rock.
It is recharged by water infiltrating directly from the surface above it, so it is vulnerable to contamination from the surface.
It cannot be depleted by pumping.
It is never connected to surface water.
questions.explanation: Water from rain and streams percolates down to the water table of an unconfined aquifer. Pumping faster than recharge lowers the water table and can cause land subsidence.

questions.stem: Coastal cities usually have milder winters and cooler summers than inland cities at the same latitude. Which best explains this?
choices: Coastal cities receive less sunlight.
Inland cities are at higher elevations.
Ocean water has a low specific heat.
Water has a high specific heat, so the ocean warms and cools slowly and moderates nearby air temperatures.
questions.explanation: Large bodies of water absorb heat in summer and release it in winter. Inland areas lack this buffering and have more extreme seasonal temperatures.

questions.stem: Many fishing fleets harvest from the same ocean fishery, and the fish population collapses. Which concept best explains this outcome?
choices: The tragedy of the commons
Integrated pest management
Carrying capacity of humans
Sustainable yield
questions.explanation: When a resource is shared and unregulated, each user gains by taking more, while the cost of overuse is spread among everyone. Quotas and catch shares can prevent this.

questions.stem: Which is a likely effect of clear-cutting a forest on a steep slope?
choices: Decreased surface runoff
Increased habitat for forest-interior species
Increased soil erosion and sediment in nearby streams
Cooler stream temperatures
questions.explanation: Removing all trees exposes soil and removes roots that hold it. Without shade, stream temperatures rise, and sediment can smother fish eggs.

questions.stem: Which is a negative consequence of the Green Revolution?
choices: Decreased crop yields
Reduced irrigation
Increased reliance on traditional crop varieties
Increased use of synthetic fertilizers and pesticides, along with loss of crop genetic diversity
questions.explanation: High-yield varieties, irrigation, fertilizers, and mechanization greatly increased food production but also increased water use, pollution, and monocultures.

figure.alt: Table of the approximate water efficiency of irrigation methods: flood 80 percent, furrow 65 percent, spray 75 percent, and drip 95 percent

questions.stem: A farm uses \(2{,}000{,}000\) liters of water per season with furrow irrigation. About how much water would be needed to deliver the same amount to the crops with drip irrigation?
choices: About \(700{,}000\) liters
questions.explanation: Furrow irrigation delivers \(0.65(2{,}000{,}000)=1{,}300{,}000\) liters to the crops. Drip irrigation must supply \(\tfrac{1{,}300{,}000}{0.95}\approx 1{,}370{,}000\) liters.

questions.stem: Over many years, an irrigated field in an arid region becomes less productive, and a white crust forms on the soil. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Waterlogging, which drowns roots
Salinization, as water evaporates and leaves salts behind
Erosion, which removes the topsoil
Nitrogen fixation, which adds salts
questions.explanation: In dry climates, irrigation water evaporates quickly, concentrating its dissolved salts in the soil. Drip irrigation and good drainage reduce salinization.

questions.stem: Based on the figure, how much more grain is needed to produce \(10\) kg of beef than \(10\) kg of chicken?
choices: \(3.5\) times as much, or \(35\) kg
questions.explanation: Beef requires \(10\times 7=70\) kg of grain and chicken requires \(10\times 2=20\) kg, a difference of \(50\) kg.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains the differences shown in the figure?
choices: Beef contains less protein than chicken.
Chickens are producers.
Cattle use much of the energy they eat for metabolism and maintaining body heat over a long life, so less is stored as meat.
Grain fed to cattle contains less energy.
questions.explanation: Energy is lost at each trophic transfer, and larger, longer-lived, warm-blooded animals convert feed into body mass less efficiently.

questions.stem: Which is a major environmental problem associated with concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs)?
choices: Manure runoff that adds nutrients and pathogens to waterways
Increased biodiversity near the facilities
Decreased use of antibiotics
Reduced demand for grain
questions.explanation: Large amounts of manure in lagoons can leak or overflow, causing eutrophication and contamination. CAFOs also emit methane and often use antibiotics heavily.

questions.stem: A farmer uses crop rotation, releases ladybugs to eat aphids, and applies a pesticide only when aphid numbers exceed a set threshold. What is this approach called?
choices: Monoculture farming
Slash-and-burn agriculture
The Green Revolution
Integrated pest management
questions.explanation: Integrated pest management combines biological, physical, and chemical methods while minimizing pesticide use, which reduces costs, pesticide resistance, and harm to nontarget organisms.

questions.stem: On a hilly farm, plowing along the contours of the slope rather than up and down it mainly reduces which problem?
choices: Pest infestations
Soil erosion by water
Salinization
Nitrogen loss to the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Contour plowing creates ridges that slow the flow of water down the slope, so less soil is carried away. Terracing and windbreaks reduce erosion in similar ways.

questions.stem: Which practice increases soil nitrogen without synthetic fertilizer?
choices: Planting the same crop every year
Rotating crops with legumes such as soybeans or clover
Removing all crop residues after harvest
Tilling the soil deeply each season
questions.explanation: Legumes host nitrogen-fixing bacteria in their root nodules. Rotating crops also disrupts pest life cycles.

questions.stem: Which fishing method causes the most damage to seafloor habitats?
choices: Pole-and-line fishing
Purse seining near the surface
Fish farming in tanks
Bottom trawling
questions.explanation: Heavy nets dragged along the bottom destroy coral, sponges, and other habitat-forming organisms, and they catch large amounts of bycatch.

questions.stem: Which describes a significant environmental impact of surface mining for coal?
choices: Removal of vegetation and overburden, which destroys habitat and can produce acid mine drainage
Increased soil fertility
Reduced erosion
Increased groundwater recharge
questions.explanation: Exposing sulfide minerals in rock to air and water forms sulfuric acid, which can leach metals into streams. Reclamation can restore some, but not all, of the land.

questions.stem: Replacing forest with pavement and buildings has which effect on a watershed?
choices: Decreased runoff and increased infiltration
Lower urban temperatures
Increased surface runoff and flooding, and decreased groundwater recharge
No effect on water flow
questions.explanation: Impervious surfaces prevent water from soaking into the ground. Runoff is faster and carries pollutants into streams, and cities become warmer than surrounding areas.

questions.stem: Which statement about ecological footprints is correct?
choices: All people have the same ecological footprint.
Footprints measure only population size.
Countries with the largest populations always have the largest footprints per person.
People in wealthy countries generally have much larger footprints, because they consume more resources and energy per person.
questions.explanation: An ecological footprint estimates the area of land and water needed to supply a person's resources and absorb their wastes. Consumption per person varies greatly between countries.

questions.stem: Which forestry practice best maintains habitat and biodiversity while still harvesting timber?
choices: Clear-cutting large areas
Replacing native forests with tree plantations of one species
Selective cutting of individual trees, leaving the rest of the forest intact
Removing all dead and fallen trees
questions.explanation: Selective cutting keeps the forest's structure and canopy. Tree plantations are monocultures with little biodiversity.

questions.stem: Which is an environmental concern of open-net salmon farming in coastal waters?
choices: It always reduces pressure on wild fish populations.
Escaped farmed fish, disease and parasites spreading to wild fish, and waste polluting the water
It requires no feed.
It increases dissolved oxygen in the water.
questions.explanation: Aquaculture can reduce pressure on wild stocks, but crowded pens concentrate wastes and pathogens. Carnivorous farmed fish are often fed fish meal from wild-caught fish.

questions.stem: A city adds green roofs, rain gardens, and permeable pavement. What is the main environmental benefit?
choices: Reduced storm water runoff and increased infiltration
Increased runoff
Higher urban temperatures
Lower groundwater recharge
questions.explanation: These features let water soak in or be absorbed by plants, reducing flooding and pollution of streams. Green roofs also reduce the urban heat island effect.

questions.stem: Slash-and-burn agriculture in tropical rainforests is usually unsustainable because:
choices: tropical soils are too rich in nutrients
burning adds nitrogen to the soil permanently
the nutrient-poor soils lose their fertility within a few years, so farmers clear new forest
crops cannot grow in warm climates
questions.explanation: Most rainforest nutrients are in the vegetation, not the soil. Ash briefly fertilizes the land, but heavy rain soon leaches the nutrients away.

questions.stem: Which is the most likely long-term result of overgrazing a semiarid grassland?
choices: Loss of vegetation cover, soil erosion, and possibly desertification
Increased soil organic matter
Greater grass diversity
Higher water infiltration
questions.explanation: Overgrazing removes plants faster than they regrow, exposing soil to wind and water erosion. Rotational grazing helps prevent this.

questions.stem: As the highest-grade ore deposits are used up, mining companies turn to lower-grade ore. What is a likely environmental consequence?
choices: Less waste is produced, because the ore is easier to process.
Mining no longer requires removing overburden.
The metal becomes more abundant in Earth's crust.
More rock must be mined and processed per kilogram of metal, producing more waste and using more energy and water.
questions.explanation: Lower-grade ores contain less metal per ton. Producing the same amount of metal requires disturbing more land and generating more tailings.

questions.stem: Which policy most directly reduces the environmental effects of urban sprawl?
choices: Building more highways to outlying suburbs
Encouraging compact, mixed-use development served by public transportation
Requiring larger minimum lot sizes
Locating housing far from jobs and shopping
questions.explanation: Compact development reduces the land converted to roads and buildings and lowers driving, cutting fuel use and air pollution.

questions.stem: The country replaces all of its coal use with natural gas while total energy use stays the same. Which is the most likely effect?
choices: Carbon dioxide emissions increase, because natural gas contains more carbon.
Emissions do not change, because both are fossil fuels.
The share of renewables increases to \(22\%\).
Carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide emissions from that energy decrease, because natural gas releases less \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) per unit of energy and little sulfur.
questions.explanation: Burning natural gas releases roughly half as much \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) per unit of energy as coal and almost no \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\) or particulates. Methane leaks during extraction and transport offset some of this benefit.

questions.stem: A power plant burns \(2.0\times 10^6\) kg of coal per day. The coal contains \(24\text{ MJ/kg}\), and the plant is \(35\%\) efficient. About how much electrical energy does it produce per day, in kilowatt-hours? (\(1\text{ kWh}=3.6\text{ MJ}\))
choices: About \(4.7\times 10^6\text{ kWh}\)
About \(1.3\times 10^7\text{ kWh}\)
About \(1.7\times 10^{13}\text{ kWh}\)
About \(4.7\times 10^3\text{ kWh}\)
questions.explanation: The coal contains \((2.0\times 10^6)(24)=4.8\times 10^7\text{ MJ}\), and \(35\%\) becomes electricity: \(1.68\times 10^7\text{ MJ}\). Dividing by \(3.6\text{ MJ/kWh}\) gives about \(4.7\times 10^6\text{ kWh}\).

questions.stem: In the power plant shown, where does most of the energy in the coal go that does not become electricity?
choices: Into the electricity, which is nearly \(100\%\) efficient
Into the chemical bonds of \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\)
Waste heat, released to the cooling water and the air
Into the turbine, where it is stored
questions.explanation: By the second law of thermodynamics, converting heat into work is never complete. Typical coal plants convert only about a third of the fuel's energy into electricity.

questions.stem: A \(60\text{ W}\) incandescent bulb is replaced by a \(9\text{ W}\) LED bulb that gives the same light. The bulb is used \(5\) hours a day for \(30\) days, and electricity costs \(\$0.20\) per kWh. How much money is saved?
questions.explanation: The savings are \(51\text{ W}\times 150\text{ h}=7{,}650\text{ Wh}=7.65\text{ kWh}\), and \(7.65\times\$0.20=\$1.53\). The value \(\$1.80\) is the cost of running the incandescent bulb.

figure.alt: Table of a wind turbine’s power output at three wind speeds: 50 kW at 4 meters per second, 400 kW at 8 meters per second, and 1,350 kW at 12 meters per second

questions.stem: Based on the table, how does the power output of the turbine depend on wind speed?
choices: It is proportional to the wind speed.
It is proportional to the square of the wind speed.
It is proportional to the cube of the wind speed: doubling the speed multiplies the power by \(8\).
It does not depend on wind speed.
questions.explanation: From \(4\) to \(8\text{ m/s}\), power rises from \(50\) to \(400\text{ kW}\), a factor of \(8=2^3\). Tripling the speed gives \(27\times 50=1{,}350\text{ kW}\). Small increases in wind speed therefore matter greatly when siting turbines.

questions.stem: Which is a significant drawback of wind power?
choices: It releases large amounts of \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) while operating.
Its output is intermittent, varying with the wind, so it requires storage or backup sources.
It requires mining and burning fuel continuously.
It produces radioactive waste.
questions.explanation: Wind turbines produce no emissions while operating, but output depends on weather. Turbines can also kill birds and bats and may face local opposition.

questions.stem: A solar panel array converts \(20\%\) of incoming sunlight to electricity. At peak sunlight of \(1{,}000\text{ W/m}^2\), what panel area is needed to produce \(5{,}000\text{ W}\)?
questions.explanation: Each square meter produces \(0.20(1{,}000)=200\text{ W}\), so \(\tfrac{5{,}000}{200}=25\text{ m}^2\) is needed.

questions.stem: Strontium-90 in nuclear waste has a half-life of about \(29\) years. How much of a \(100\text{ g}\) sample remains after \(87\) years?
questions.explanation: Eighty-seven years is three half-lives: \(100\to 50\to 25\to 12.5\text{ g}\). Long half-lives are why spent fuel must be stored safely for very long periods.

questions.stem: Which statement about nuclear power plants is correct?
choices: They release almost no \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) while operating, but they produce long-lived radioactive waste and thermal pollution.
They burn uranium in combustion reactions.
They produce large amounts of \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\).
They generate electricity without using turbines.
questions.explanation: Fission of uranium-235 releases heat that boils water to drive turbines, like a fossil fuel plant. The major concerns are waste storage, accidents, and the cost of construction.

questions.stem: Which is an environmental impact of building a large hydroelectric dam?
choices: Release of large amounts of sulfur dioxide
Increased sediment delivery to downstream deltas
Faster-flowing rivers downstream that carry more nutrients
Flooding of land upstream and blocking of fish migration, with sediment trapped behind the dam
questions.explanation: Reservoirs flood habitats and can release methane from decaying vegetation. Trapped sediment deprives downstream areas of soil and causes deltas to erode.

questions.stem: Which is a major environmental concern of hydraulic fracturing (fracking) for natural gas?
choices: Release of large amounts of ozone into the stratosphere
Contamination of groundwater and leaks of methane, a potent greenhouse gas
Depletion of the ozone layer
Production of radioactive spent fuel rods
questions.explanation: Fracking injects water, sand, and chemicals at high pressure to fracture rock. Wastewater disposal, methane leaks, large water use, and induced earthquakes are concerns.

questions.stem: A car that gets \(25\) miles per gallon is driven \(12{,}000\) miles a year. Burning one gallon of gasoline releases about \(8.9\text{ kg}\) of \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\). How much \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) does the car emit in a year?
choices: About \(107{,}000\text{ kg}\)
About \(4{,}300\text{ kg}\)
About \(480\text{ kg}\)
About \(2{,}700\text{ kg}\)
questions.explanation: The car uses \(\tfrac{12{,}000}{25}=480\) gallons, emitting \(480(8.9)\approx 4{,}300\text{ kg}\) of \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\).

questions.stem: Which statement about hydrogen fuel cells is correct?
choices: They burn hydrogen in a combustion engine, releasing \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\).
Hydrogen gas is freely available in large natural deposits.
They require uranium to operate.
They combine hydrogen and oxygen to produce electricity, with water as the main product, but hydrogen is often made from natural gas.
questions.explanation: A fuel cell's only direct product is water. Its environmental benefit depends on how the hydrogen is produced; electrolysis using renewable electricity avoids carbon emissions.

questions.stem: Which statement about geothermal energy is correct?
choices: It uses heat from Earth's interior and is most practical near tectonic plate boundaries.
It is available equally everywhere.
It relies on burning underground coal.
It produces energy only during daylight.
questions.explanation: Places such as Iceland have hot rock close to the surface. Ground-source heat pumps, however, can use the steady temperature of shallow ground almost anywhere.

questions.stem: Which is a drawback of burning wood or crop residues for energy in homes?
choices: It produces radioactive waste.
It releases no carbon dioxide.
Indoor air pollution, including particulates and carbon monoxide, along with deforestation if harvesting is not sustainable
It cannot be used in developing countries.
questions.explanation: In many developing countries, indoor smoke from cooking fires is a leading cause of respiratory disease. Biomass is renewable only if it is regrown as fast as it is used.

questions.stem: Which approach to heating a building uses energy most efficiently?
choices: Electric resistance heaters powered by a coal plant
Leaving windows open in winter
Using incandescent bulbs for heat
Cogeneration, using the waste heat from electricity generation to heat buildings
questions.explanation: Using waste heat that would otherwise be lost can raise overall efficiency well above that of a power plant alone.

questions.stem: Which energy source is renewable?
choices: Coal
Natural gas
Solar power
Uranium for nuclear fission
questions.explanation: Renewable sources are replenished on human time scales. Fossil fuels form over millions of years, and uranium ore is finite.

questions.stem: How does energy use per person generally compare between highly developed and less developed countries?
choices: It is higher in less developed countries.
It is much higher in highly developed countries.
It is the same everywhere.
It is unrelated to economic development.
questions.explanation: Industrialized economies use far more energy per person for transportation, industry, and homes, although developing countries' energy use is growing quickly.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts tidal power with solar power?
choices: Tidal power is highly predictable, but it is feasible at only a few coastal sites.
Tidal power is available in every inland location.
Solar power is more predictable than tidal power.
Tidal power releases large amounts of \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\).
questions.explanation: Tides follow the moon's cycle, so tidal output can be forecast years ahead. Few coastlines have tidal ranges large enough to make it practical.

questions.stem: Which change would most reduce the energy use of an average home in a cold climate?
choices: Using a slightly smaller refrigerator
Unplugging phone chargers
Adding insulation and sealing air leaks
Switching to cold-water laundry only
questions.explanation: Heating is typically the largest share of home energy use in cold climates, and most heat escapes through poorly insulated walls, roofs, windows, and air leaks.

questions.stem: Which describes a concern about extracting oil from tar sands?
choices: It requires large amounts of energy and water, and it disturbs large areas of land.
It produces cleaner fuel than conventional oil.
It has no impact on water supplies.
It produces no greenhouse gases.
questions.explanation: Separating bitumen from sand takes heat and water and leaves tailings ponds. The extra energy used means higher emissions per barrel than conventional oil.

figure.alt: Concentrations of three air pollutants over a sunny day in a city. Pollutant X peaks sharply near 8 a.m. with a smaller peak near 6 p.m. Pollutant Y peaks near 10:30 a.m. Pollutant Z peaks in the afternoon near 2:30 p.m. and is low at night

questions.stem: Which pollutants are most likely represented by X, Y, and Z in the graph?
choices: X is ozone, Y is NO, and Z is \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\).
X is \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\), Y is ozone, and Z is NO.
X, Y, and Z are all primary pollutants emitted by cars.
X is nitrogen oxide (NO), Y is nitrogen dioxide (\(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\)), and Z is ground-level ozone (\(\mathrm{O_{3}}\)).
questions.explanation: Vehicles emit NO during the morning commute. It oxidizes to \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\), and sunlight breaks \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\) apart, producing ozone that peaks in the afternoon.

figure.alt: Concentrations of three air pollutants over a sunny day in a city. Pollutant X peaks sharply near 8 a.m. with a smaller peak near 6 p.m. Pollutant Y peaks near 10:30 a.m. Pollutant Z peaks in the afternoon near 2:30 p.m. and is low at night

questions.stem: Why does pollutant Z in the graph decrease after sunset?
choices: More vehicles are on the road in the evening.
Without sunlight, no new ozone forms, and existing ozone reacts with NO and other substances.
Ozone is a primary pollutant that stops being emitted at night.
Ozone rises into the stratosphere at night.
questions.explanation: Photochemical smog depends on sunlight. At night, ozone is consumed by reactions with NO from evening traffic.

questions.stem: Which is a secondary pollutant?
choices: Carbon monoxide
Ground-level ozone
Sulfur dioxide
Particulate matter from a diesel engine
questions.explanation: Secondary pollutants form in the atmosphere from reactions among primary pollutants. Ozone forms when \(\mathrm{NO_x}\) and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight.

choices: Pollutants rise and disperse more quickly than usual.
Strong winds blow pollutants away.
Rain removes the pollutants.
Pollutants near the ground are trapped, because the warm layer above prevents cooler, polluted air from rising.
